[id="configuring-persistent-state-langgraph-agents_{context}"]
= Configure persistent state for LangGraph agents on {productname-short}

[role="_abstract"]
You can configure persistent state for a LangGraph agent running on {productname-long} so that conversation history and agent checkpoints survive pod restarts and scaling events.
By transitioning from local in-memory or SQLite storage to PostgreSQL, you ensure that your agent retains context across the full pod lifecycle.

.Prerequisites

* A LangGraph agent is deployed to {productname-short}. See xref:deploying-langgraph-agent-to-rhoai_{context}[Deploy a LangGraph agent from local development to {productname-short}].
* A PostgreSQL 14 or later instance is accessible from the agent pod. See xref:configuring-postgresql-langgraph-agent-state_{context}[Configure PostgreSQL for LangGraph agent state persistence].
* You have the PostgreSQL connection credentials (host, port, database name, username, and password).
* You are logged in to the {openshift-platform} cluster with the {openshift-cli} (`oc`).

.Procedure

. Identify the current local state backend in your agent application.
+
Check your `run.yaml` file for the `providers.agents` section.
A local development configuration typically uses SQLite:
+
[source,yaml]
----
providers:
  agents:
  - provider_id: meta-reference
    provider_type: inline::meta-reference
    config:
      persistence_store:
        type: sqlite
        db_path: ${env.SQLITE_STORE_DIR:=~/.llama/distributions/custom}/agents_store.db
      responses_store:
        type: sqlite
        db_path: ${env.SQLITE_STORE_DIR:=~/.llama/distributions/custom}/responses_store.db
----
+
Also check your agent application code for the checkpointer class.
Local development typically uses `MemorySaver`:
+
[source,python]
----
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver
checkpointer = MemorySaver()  # Local development only -- do not use in production
----

. Update the Llama Stack `run.yaml` to use PostgreSQL for agent metadata storage.
+
Replace the `persistence_store` and `responses_store` sections with PostgreSQL configuration:
+
[source,yaml]
----
providers:
  agents:
  - provider_id: meta-reference
    provider_type: inline::meta-reference
    config:
      persistence_store:
        type: postgres
        host: ${env.POSTGRES_HOST}
        port: ${env.POSTGRES_PORT:=5432}
        db: ${env.POSTGRES_DB}
        user: ${env.POSTGRES_USER}
        password: ${env.POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      responses_store:
        type: postgres
        host: ${env.POSTGRES_HOST}
        port: ${env.POSTGRES_PORT:=5432}
        db: ${env.POSTGRES_DB}
        user: ${env.POSTGRES_USER}
        password: ${env.POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
----

. Update the LangGraph checkpointer in your agent application code.
+
Replace the `MemorySaver` checkpointer with `PostgresSaver` to persist graph checkpoints in PostgreSQL.
+
Install version 2.0 or later of the `langgraph-checkpoint-postgres` package:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ uv add langgraph-checkpoint-postgres
----
+
Alternatively, if your project does not use `uv`, install the package with `pip`:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ pip install langgraph-checkpoint-postgres
----
+
Update your agent application code to use the `PostgresSaver` class with the context manager pattern:
+
[source,python]
----
from langgraph.checkpoint.postgres import PostgresSaver

conn_string = f"postgresql://{POSTGRES_USER}:{POSTGRES_PASSWORD}@{POSTGRES_HOST}:{POSTGRES_PORT}/{POSTGRES_DB}"

with PostgresSaver.from_conn_string(conn_string) as checkpointer:
    checkpointer.setup()
    graph = workflow.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer)
----
+
The `with` statement ensures that the underlying database connection is properly closed when the block exits.
Without the context manager, database connections are leaked on each initialization, which can exhaust the PostgreSQL connection pool in long-running agent processes.
+
The `setup()` method creates checkpoint tables if they do not already exist.
It is safe to call on every application startup.
The PostgreSQL user must have `CREATE TABLE` privileges on the target database.
+
For high-concurrency production deployments, consider using `psycopg_pool.ConnectionPool` to manage database connections instead of a single connection.
See the link:https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/concepts/persistence/[LangGraph persistence documentation] for connection pooling patterns.
+
[NOTE]
====
If you prefer Redis for checkpoint storage, install `langgraph-checkpoint-redis` and use the `RedisSaver` class instead.
Redis provides lower latency for high-throughput workloads but does not replace the Llama Stack metadata store, which still requires PostgreSQL.
====

. Set the PostgreSQL connection environment variables in the Helm values file.
+
Add the PostgreSQL connection parameters to the `env` section of your Helm `values.yaml`:
+
[source,yaml]
----
env:
  POSTGRES_HOST: "<postgres_host>"
  POSTGRES_PORT: "5432"
  POSTGRES_DB: "<postgres_database>"
  POSTGRES_USER: "<postgres_user>"
  POSTGRES_PASSWORD: "<postgres_password>"
----
+
--
Where:

`<postgres_host>`:: Specifies the hostname or Kubernetes service URL of the PostgreSQL instance. If you deployed PostgreSQL by using the preceding procedure, use `postgresql.<postgres_namespace>.svc.cluster.local`, where `<postgres_namespace>` is the namespace of the PostgreSQL deployment.
`<postgres_database>`:: Specifies the name of the database created for agent state storage.
`<postgres_user>`:: Specifies the PostgreSQL user with read and write access to the database.
`<postgres_password>`:: Specifies the password for the PostgreSQL user.
--
+
[IMPORTANT]
====
The plain text credentials shown here are suitable for development only.
For production deployments, store database credentials in a Kubernetes `Secret` and reference them in your Helm values by using `valueFrom.secretKeyRef`.
Do not commit plain text passwords to source control.

The following example shows the production-safe pattern by using `valueFrom.secretKeyRef`:

[source,yaml]
----
env:
  - name: POSTGRES_HOST
    value: "<postgres_host>"
  - name: POSTGRES_PORT
    value: "5432"
  - name: POSTGRES_DB
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: postgresql-credentials
        key: POSTGRESQL_DATABASE
  - name: POSTGRES_USER
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: postgresql-credentials
        key: POSTGRESQL_USER
  - name: POSTGRES_PASSWORD
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: postgresql-credentials
        key: POSTGRESQL_PASSWORD
----

The `react_with_database_memory` agent variant in the agentic starter kits also demonstrates this pattern.
====

. Redeploy the agent with the updated configuration.
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ helm upgrade <release_name> charts/agent/ -f my-values.yaml -n <namespace>
----
+
--
Where:

`<release_name>`:: Specifies the Helm release name for your agent deployment.
`<namespace>`:: Specifies the OpenShift project where the agent is deployed.
--

.Verification

. Verify that the agent pod starts successfully with the new configuration:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc get pods -n <namespace> -l app=<release_name>
----

. Send a test request to the agent to create a conversation and note the returned `thread_id` or submission ID:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ curl -X POST http://<agent_route>/submit-question \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "question=What is the Apache 2.0 license?"
----
+
Record the `thread_id` value from the response.
+
[NOTE]
====
The `/submit-question` and `/get-response` endpoints are specific to the agentic starter kits.
If you built a custom agent application, substitute your application's equivalent endpoints.
====

. Restart the agent pod to simulate a pod lifecycle event:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ oc delete pod -n <namespace> -l app=<release_name>
----
+
Wait for the new pod to reach `Running` status.

. Send a follow-up request using the same `thread_id` from step 2 to verify that conversation state persisted:
+
[source,terminal]
----
$ curl -X POST http://<agent_route>/submit-question \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "question=Can you summarize what we discussed?" \
  -d "thread_id=<thread_id_from_step_2>"
----
+
--
Where:

`<thread_id_from_step_2>`:: Specifies the `thread_id` value returned by the initial request in step 2.
--
+
The agent references the earlier conversation about the Apache 2.0 license, confirming that state persisted in PostgreSQL across the pod restart.
